newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian jobs marchers slam Euro-inhumanity.
newsitem.headline: Belgian jobs marchers slam Euro-inhumanity.

text.p: Tens of thousands of European trades unionists and politicians turned central Brussels into a sea of colour and noise on Sunday as they vented their anger at rising job losses, inhumane firms and uncaring governments.
"This is a signal af anger and indignation. A signal of solidarity against brutality," Willy Peirens, head of Belgium's Christian Democratic CSC union, told the crowd.
"We don't want to be lied to again. We won't be cheated again," he said.
The crowd was awash with red, green, yellow and blue union banners and balloons, the air rent by ear-shattering whistles and firecrackers, chanting, sirens and megaphones.
"For swine fever they follow more rules than for us," one banner read, succinctly summing up the general mood.

French carmaker Renault and chairman Louis Schweitzer came in for particularly harsh treatment after the firm's shock decision two weeks ago to close its profitable plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
"Renault is developing turbo-charged unemployment," one banner read.
Schweitzer was hung in effigy. A giant wickerwork figure made Nazi salutes. Vilvoorde workers dumped a yellow car body in front of the Brussels bourse and stamped on it before moving on.

The leading marchers reached the end at Brussels South Station long before everyone who wanted to join in had left the start at North Station three kilometres (1.8 miles) away. More than three hours after the march began, demonstrators were still parading past the bourse, half way along the route.

Police said at least 50,000 people turned up for the rally, while union organisers -- who said it was the first truly pan-European march -- put the figure at 120,000. More than 500 police and 1,000 gendarmes were on the streets.

"What Renault did was disgusting. We did our best. We did everything they asked for," said Vilvoorde worker Jan De Koninck, 33. "Perhaps for Vilvoorde it is too late but we are now starting something to change the situation in Europe."

Unemployment, a seeping sore as the 15 European Union nations slash their budgets and raise taxes in the struggle to ready their economies for joining the bloc's single currency in 1999, has become a uniting force.
"We need a better balance in the European economic and social model. It has gone too far in liberalisation," French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin told Reuters.
The Renault closure news followed the bankruptcy in January of Belgian steelmaker Forges de Clabecq, threatening 1,800 jobs.
Unions said there were delegations from France, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Austria, Hungary, Slovenia and the Czech Republic.
"It is a show of solidarity. We are all workers. We are all in the struggle," said Stewart Davis, 22, who came with a delegation from the Rolls Royce plant at Bristol in Britain.
"We are here to express our solidarity with the workers of Belgium," Manuel Zaguirre Cano, a Spanish union official said. "We have to fight on the European level."
Newspapers said Renault sales in Belgium had fallen 40 percent since the closure news. A Renault salesman from Austria, who asked to remain anonymous, said sales were down 15 percent.
Unemployment in the 15-nation European Union is stuck at 10.8 percent of the workforce, with most governments apparently unable to tackle the social crisis.

The unions want consultations with employers on working hours, and for governments to cut the tax costs of employment and introduce tax policies that encourage jobs, a coherent social policy and moves to encourage economic growth.
EU social affairs ministers who met in Rotterdam at the weekend said there should be a clear code of conduct for multinationals both opening and closing factories.
But with the decision day on who will be in the vanguard of nations joining the single currency less than a year away, countries are tightening their belts in a bid to join the club.
